questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the single most common real-world path into multi-cloud?
options: A marketing requirement to appear vendor-neutral to customers
A cloud provider requires customers to also use a second provider by contract
An architecture team decides in the abstract that two providers are safer than one
An acquisition brings in a company that already built its stack on a different cloud
questions.explain: Multi-cloud by inheritance — a merger or acquisition bringing in an estate built on a different provider — is the most common way organizations actually end up running more than one cloud, not a deliberate strategy chosen up front.

questions.q: Which of the following is presented as a genuinely defensible best-of-breed driver for multi-cloud?
options: A specific capability gap for a specific workload that one provider closes meaningfully better than the others, justifying the integration cost
A desire to spend the same amount on every provider for fairness
A rule that every new project must use a different cloud than the last one
A team wants to list two providers on their resume
questions.explain: Best-of-breed multi-cloud is justified when a named, specific capability gap exists for a specific workload and the value of closing it outweighs the integration cost — not a generic preference for variety.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call 'we don't want to be locked into one vendor,' said with no further detail, an anxiety rather than a reason?
options: Because only small companies need to worry about lock-in
Because every cloud provider contractually guarantees portability
Because it names no specific service, scenario, or cost comparison, so it can't be evaluated against the real cost of running two clouds
Because vendor lock-in has been proven to never actually happen
questions.explain: Without a specific capability, scenario, or cost analysis attached, 'avoid lock-in' can't be weighed against the real, ongoing cost of multi-cloud — it's an unquantified fear, not a requirement.

questions.q: In the three-question test this lesson gives for evaluating a proposed multi-cloud initiative, what must question 1 identify?
options: Which cloud provider is currently cheapest on list price
A specific capability, constraint, or event driving the need — not a generic fear of dependence
How many engineers are already certified on each provider
Whether the CEO has a personal preference for a particular vendor
questions.explain: The first question forces the proposer to name a concrete driver — an acquisition, a service gap, a regulatory requirement, or a disaster scenario — rather than accept 'lock-in' as a standalone justification.

questions.q: Why does the lesson describe genuine disaster-recovery independence across two providers as legitimate but still something to apply selectively?
options: Because it is real protection against provider-level outages, but it is genuinely expensive, so it should be reserved for workloads where that cost is actually justified
Because it is illegal in most jurisdictions
Because no cloud provider allows cross-provider DR under its terms of service
Because it only works for workloads smaller than a single virtual machine
questions.explain: DR independence across providers is a legitimate reason to go multi-cloud, but because it carries real, ongoing cost, the lesson argues it should be applied to specific critical workloads rather than blanket-wide.
